meta.titre: Judaism: covenant, scriptures and the Jewish groups of the Second Temple period
meta.sous_theme: Core Jewish beliefs, writings, practices and the sects of Jesus' time

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Religious Studies past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Many of the people you meet in church readings, such as Abraham, Moses, David and Daniel, belong first to the story of the Jewish people. To read the Old Testament and the world of Jesus with understanding, you need to know what Jews believe, which writings they honour and which groups competed for influence in Palestine under Roman rule. The GCE paper asks short factual questions about names and groups, and longer questions that ask you to compare beliefs fairly.

items: Jews trace their origin to Abraham, with whom they believe God made a covenant.
The books of the Hebrew Bible form the core of the Christian Old Testament.
A sect is a group within a religion that holds its own distinctive interpretation of the faith.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Core beliefs and practices
- **One God**: Judaism is monotheistic; God is creator and lawgiver.
- **Covenant**: Jews believe that God made a covenant with Abraham and renewed it with the people at Sinai through Moses, so that Israel lives by the Torah.
- **Scriptures**: the Tanakh has three parts: the Torah (the five books of Moses), the Nevi'im (Prophets) and the Ketuvim (Writings). The Talmud, made up of the Mishnah and the Gemara, records rabbinic discussion of the law handed down by tradition.
- **Maimonides**: the twelfth-century rabbi and philosopher Moses Maimonides summarised the faith in thirteen principles, including belief in the existence and unity of God, that the Torah comes from God, in the coming of the Messiah, in the resurrection of the dead, and in reward and punishment. Do not confuse him with the prophet Moses.
- **Practice**: the Sabbath from Friday evening to Saturday evening, worship in the synagogue led by a rabbi, circumcision of baby boys on the eighth day, food laws (kashrut), and festivals such as Passover, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot and Hanukkah. Passover recalls the liberation from Egypt and Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement.

### Exile and the Second Temple period
In the sixth century BCE the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar conquered Judah, destroyed the first Temple in Jerusalem and took many Jews into exile. The Book of Daniel presents Daniel as a Jewish exile at the Babylonian court who interpreted the king's dreams. The Temple was later rebuilt, and in Jesus' time Palestine was ruled by Rome. The Romans destroyed the rebuilt Temple in 70 CE.

### Jewish groups in the time of Jesus
| Group | Main features |
|---|---|
| Pharisees | Accepted the oral tradition as well as the written law, taught in the synagogues and believed in the resurrection of the dead and in angels. |
| Sadducees | Associated with the priestly families and the Temple; accepted only the written law and denied the resurrection. |
| Essenes | A strict, separatist movement living in communities apart from society; often linked with the Dead Sea Scrolls found near Qumran. |
| Zealots | An extreme nationalist group that wanted to end Roman rule by force; active in the Jewish revolt against Rome of 66 to 70 CE. |

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to compare or distinguish two Jewish groups.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Compare on fixed headings: authority (written law only or also the oral tradition), attitude to the Temple, belief in resurrection and angels, and attitude to Roman rule. Always state both groups under each heading.

variantes.quand_utiliser: In Paper 1 when one name is required.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Link each name with one fact: Daniel with the dreams of Nebuchadnezzar, Maimonides with the thirteen principles of faith, the Zealots with violent nationalism, the Sadducees with the Temple and the denial of resurrection.

sections.enonce_markdown: Compare the beliefs of the Pharisees and the Sadducees. (10 marks)

etapes.justification: 'Compare' requires similarities and differences on the same points, not two separate descriptions.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Both groups are Jewish sects of the same period; the answer must set them side by side.
Authority of the law, resurrection and angels, relation to the Temple.

etapes.justification: A good comparison states what is shared.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Both accepted the Torah as God's law and both took part in the religious life of Judaism in Palestine.

etapes.action: Write the differences under each heading.
etapes.justification: Each difference should name both groups.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Pharisees accepted the oral tradition and Sadducees only the written law; Pharisees believed in resurrection and Sadducees denied it; Sadducees were linked with the priests and Temple while Pharisees taught in synagogues.

etapes.justification: A conclusion states the main contrast.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Their central disagreement was over the authority of tradition and the hope of resurrection.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** The Pharisees and the Sadducees were two Jewish groups in Palestine in the time of Jesus. They were alike in accepting the Torah as God's law and in sharing a concern for Jewish religious life. They differed in several ways. The Pharisees accepted the oral tradition as well as the written law, whereas the Sadducees accepted only the written law. The Pharisees believed in the resurrection of the dead and in angels, but the Sadducees denied the resurrection. The Sadducees were associated with the priestly families and the Temple in Jerusalem, while the Pharisees taught in the synagogues. The main contrast between them was therefore the authority of tradition and the hope of life after death.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that the Sadducees believed in the resurrection.
items.pourquoi_faux: They denied it; it was a Pharisaic belief.
items.correction_markdown: Write that the Pharisees believed in resurrection and the Sadducees did not.

items.erreur_markdown: Attributing the thirteen principles of faith to the prophet Moses.
items.pourquoi_faux: They were formulated by Moses Maimonides in the twelfth century CE, long after the prophet Moses.
items.correction_markdown: Credit the thirteen principles to Maimonides.

items.erreur_markdown: Treating the Zealots as a purely religious group of teachers like the Pharisees.
items.pourquoi_faux: The Zealots were known mainly as extreme nationalists who wanted to remove Roman rule by force.
items.correction_markdown: Describe the Zealots as a nationalist sect whose resistance to Rome was also religiously motivated.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that Jews accept Jesus as the Messiah.
items.pourquoi_faux: Judaism does not accept that Jesus was the Messiah, although Christians do. The answer must describe each tradition in its own terms.
items.correction_markdown: Write 'Christians believe that Jesus is the Messiah, but Jews continue to await the Messiah'.

items.erreur_markdown: Mixing the destruction of the Temple by Nebuchadnezzar with its destruction by the Romans.
items.pourquoi_faux: They are different events more than six centuries apart.
items.correction_markdown: Place the Babylonian destruction in the sixth century BCE and the Roman destruction in 70 CE.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the three parts of the Tanakh and say what the Talmud contains.
items.solution_markdown: The Tanakh has the **Torah, the Nevi'im and the Ketuvim**. The Talmud contains the Mishnah and the Gemara, the rabbinic discussion of the law.

items.enonce_markdown: Describe the main features of the Essenes and explain how they differed from the Sadducees. (8 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Essenes: a strict, separatist movement living in communities apart from society, often linked with the Dead Sea Scrolls found near Qumran (up to 4 marks). Difference: the Sadducees were associated with the priestly families and the Temple, whereas the Essenes withdrew from society into their own communities (up to 4 marks). **Award 4 marks for the description and 4 marks for a clear contrast.**

items.enonce_markdown: To what extent was the movement of the Zealots a religious rather than a political one? (15 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Political case: the Zealots wanted to end Roman rule by force and took part in the revolt of 66 to 70 CE. Religious case: many believed that only God should rule Israel, so submission to a foreign power seemed to betray the covenant, and they were concerned to defend the Temple and the Torah. Evaluation: in this period religion and politics were closely joined, so the two motives cannot be fully separated. **Conclusion: the Zealots were a political movement with a religious basis, so neither label alone is complete.** Award marks for both sides, accurate knowledge and a reasoned judgement.

items_markdown: Judaism teaches one God and a covenant with Israel, shown in the Torah.
The Tanakh consists of the Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim; the Talmud contains the Mishnah and the Gemara.
Maimonides summarised Jewish belief in thirteen principles; he is not the prophet Moses.
Pharisees accepted oral tradition and resurrection; Sadducees, linked with the Temple, accepted only the written law and denied resurrection.
Essenes lived apart in strict communities; Zealots were extreme nationalists who resisted Rome by force.
In comparison questions, use common headings and describe each tradition in its own terms.
